What this site is#Redstonetics is my personal portfolio and lab. I explore how data systems are designed, built, and connected.
The work here explores how different layers of a system fit together, from infrastructure and platforms to automation and analytics.
This site also serves as a personal lab: a place to experiment, document ideas, and turn learning into working systems.
It also acts as a personal workbench to combat procrastination — helping me turn learning into projects and build momentum through public, incremental progress!
What you’ll find#My Work
Use Cases: practical ideas translated into real implementations Cloud Architecture: System Design, Platform Decision, TOGAF and architectural trade-offs Projects : Personal interests and self-driven work, embracing open source to build meaningful projects.
Writings: Notes, tutorials, concepts, patterns, and lessons learned along the way
Books :Personal reading and takeaways — ideas, stories, and lessons that inspire me.
Categories : organized ways to explore my work
Tags : quick reference keywords
Me : background, career story, expertise, and key projects
Philosophy#Redstonetics is guided by a simple belief:
quoteSystems exist to serve users, not complexity. They must remain understandable and maintainable.
Architecture is not about chasing trends or drawing perfect diagrams — it’s about reliability, clarity, and working within real constraints: people, cost, complexity, and failure.
I also believe:
quoteSystems evolve over time, and architectural patterns should be applied intentionally. Microservices and distributed designs are powerful tools, but they make sense only when scale, team structure, or operational needs truly require them — not simply by choice or trend.
Some of the most dependable/monolith systems in the world favor stability over novelty:
Banks continue to rely on COBOL-based cores. GitHub, Stack Overflow, and Shopify still run largely as a monolith. Airbnb evolved gradually from a monolith, adopted more service-oriented designs as they grew. These examples illustrate a simple principle: build what works, observe how it behaves, and evolve intentionally.

Soon Kien Yuan#I’m a platform engineer who builds and runs data systems. Redstonetics is my lab — where I turn ideas into working infrastructure.
This timeline shows how I got here. How I got into building systemsEarly yearsFinalYearProjectI started with my bachelor Degree’s industry-collaboration data science project: "Self-Service Analytics data lakehouse" using Dremio as the data platform.
The project itself was far from perfect — my work and paper were rough and not very production-ready — but it showed me something important:
Real data systems are not just about design and technologyThey depend on platforms, infrastructure, and how people actually use themThat experience sparked my curiosity and led me toward:
InfrastructureAutomationCloud-based data platforms and architectureThat opportunity grew my curiostiy and grew into a focus on infrastructure, automation, and eventually data platforms and cloud architecture First production systems2023From scripts to platformsMy first real-world project was building a Network Data Platform for a telecommunications company’s Network Analytics & Intelligence team.
I worked with enterprise-scale Azure environments, including:
Microsoft Cloud Adoption FrameworkConnectivity, Management, and Application Landing Zone I learned & built an end-to-end ML platform (Azure ML) that enabled data scientists to:
Transition models from pickle files to MLflow Enabled experiment tracking and metadata logging for reproducibilitycentralized Model Registry for versioning and governanceTrack metadata and experiment logsDevelopment and serving environments so data scientists could train and deploy models on cost-efficient compute/endpoint Read moreI also learned and built a serverless lakehouse to support SQL-based analytics on the data lake:
Enabled downstream analytics and applicationsSupported a modern lakehouse-style data architectureTo ensure enterprise-grade reliability and security, I Learnt and implemented:
Azure Defender for Cloud across VM and Azure EnvCentralized secrets and key managementCentralized Log collection & Analytics and forwarding to the customer’s SIEM EnvSAST and security scanning for all Terraform code for compliance assuranceThis is where infrastructure, data engineering, and architecture come together into systems teams can actually use.
↑ Show lessCloud Engineering & Data PlatformPresentPlatforms, Data, and DevOpsI currently design, build, and operate data platforms on AzureMy work spans the full platform lifecycle:
Designing Azure Cloud architecure, Landing Zone (networking, identity, isolation, security)Building data platforms from ingestion to analyticsAutomating everything with Terraform, CI/CD, and policy-driven governanceDesigning data flows and medallion architectures (raw → curated → consumer → Dashboard or Database)I design storage and network boundaries intentionally:
Landing storage accounts live in subnets exposed to data sources (internet or on-prem)Raw, structured, curated, and consumer zones live in private subnets, isolated from direct external accessData moves inward through controlled pipelines, not open endpointsRead moreWhen data engineers are not available, I also work at the data-ingestion and pipeline layer:
Writing Python scripts to pull data from APIs and sourcesOrchestrating and scheduling pipelines using Azure Data FactoryOn a typical platform I work across:
Networking & isolation (hub-spoke, private endpoints, segmented subnets)Compute & PaaS (VMs, managed services, Kubernetes when appropriate)Data flows (ingestion → raw → curated → consumer)Security & governance (IAM, secrets, logging, compliance, cost controls)I focus on building platforms that are:
Operable (easy to run, monitor, and troubleshoot)Cost-awareSafe to changeThis is where infrastructure, data engineering, and architecture come together into systems teams can actually use.
↑ Show lessRedstonetics — my labOngoingLearning by building, build the Systems that workRedstonetics is where I turn learning into working systems. I use it to document experiments, write about failures, and build small but real projects — not demos, but systems that run.
Beyond cloud infrastructure, I explore how data systems behave in the real world — outside of vendor platforms and managed services.
This includes working with:
Open-source data platformsSelf-hosted data stacks on VMs and KubernetesOn-prem, hybrid, and low-cost cloud environmentsI build and test how:
Data moves from raw sources into analytical modelsMetadata, lineage, and quality are managedFailures, retries, and backfills actually behaveIt keeps my work grounded in reality — not just in diagrams or vendor architectures, but in systems that engineers and analysts can actually run and trust.
Where I’m goingFuturePrincipal platform engineer?My goal is to become a principal platform engineer, specializing in building and running data systems.
I want to work across:
Public cloud, private cloud, and on-prem environmentsOpen-source Infrastructure, platforms, and data pipelinesI care about systems that:
Actually work and provide real valueEasy for teams to operate, without vendor lock-inSurvive real-world usage, load, and mistakes
